# Editorial overview

| Problem | Preprocessing | Query |
|---|---|---|
| A. Prime Counter | prime sieve + prefix | range prime count |
| B. Factor Signature | smallest prime factor | factor statistics |
| C. Divisor Queries | smallest prime factor | divisor count |

# A. Prime Counter

## Restatement

Count primes in many intervals `[l,r]`.

## Algorithm

Build `is_prime` with the sieve of Eratosthenes, then build:

```text
pref[i] = pref[i-1] + is_prime[i]
```

Answer each query by `pref[r] - pref[l-1]`.

## Correctness proof

The sieve marks a composite number when processing one of its prime divisors.
Every composite `x` has a prime divisor at most `sqrt(x)`, so it is marked.
No prime is ever marked, because a prime has no smaller divisor. Thus
`is_prime` is correct.

The prefix array counts primes up to each position, so subtracting counts before
`l` leaves exactly the primes in `[l,r]`. `\square`

## Complexity

```text
Preprocessing: O(n log log n)
Each query:   O(1)
Memory:       O(n)
```

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    int n, q;
    if (!(cin >> n >> q)) return 0;
    vector<bool> is_prime(n + 1, true);
    if (n >= 0) is_prime[0] = false;
    if (n >= 1) is_prime[1] = false;
    for (long long p = 2; p * p <= n; p++) {
        if (is_prime[p]) {
            for (long long x = p * p; x <= n; x += p) is_prime[x] = false;
        }
    }
    vector<int> pref(n + 1, 0);
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) pref[i] = pref[i - 1] + is_prime[i];
    while (q--) {
        int l, r;
        cin >> l >> r;
        cout << pref[r] - pref[l - 1] << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys


def sieve(n: int) -> list[bool]:
    is_prime = [True] * (n + 1)
    if n >= 0:
        is_prime[0] = False
    if n >= 1:
        is_prime[1] = False
    p = 2
    while p * p <= n:
        if is_prime[p]:
            for x in range(p * p, n + 1, p):
                is_prime[x] = False
        p += 1
    return is_prime


def main() -> None:
    data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
    if not data:
        return
    n, q = data[0], data[1]
    is_prime = sieve(n)
    pref = [0] * (n + 1)
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        pref[i] = pref[i - 1] + int(is_prime[i])
    idx = 2
    out = []
    for _ in range(q):
        l, r = data[idx], data[idx + 1]
        idx += 2
        out.append(str(pref[r] - pref[l - 1]))
    print("\n".join(out))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

# B. Factor Signature

## Restatement

For each `x`, print the number of distinct prime factors, the total number of
prime factors with multiplicity, and the largest prime factor.

## Algorithm

Build `spf` up to the maximum query value. For each `x`, repeatedly take
`p = spf[x]`, count how many times it divides `x`, and divide it out.

## Correctness proof

`spf[x]` is a prime divisor of `x`, and specifically the smallest one. Dividing
out all copies of `spf[x]` records exactly one distinct factor and its exponent.
Repeating until `x=1` records every prime-power block in the unique prime
factorization. The requested statistics are direct sums over those blocks.
`\square`

## Complexity

```text
Preprocessing: O(N log log N)
Each query:   O(number of prime factors)
```

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    int q;
    if (!(cin >> q)) return 0;
    vector<int> values(q);
    int mx = 1;
    for (int &x : values) {
        cin >> x;
        mx = max(mx, x);
    }
    vector<int> spf(mx + 1);
    iota(spf.begin(), spf.end(), 0);
    if (mx >= 1) spf[1] = 1;
    for (long long p = 2; p <= mx; p++) {
        if (spf[p] == p && p * p <= mx) {
            for (long long x = p * p; x <= mx; x += p) {
                if (spf[x] == x) spf[x] = p;
            }
        }
    }
    for (int x0 : values) {
        if (x0 == 1) {
            cout << "0 0 1\n";
            continue;
        }
        int x = x0, distinct = 0, total = 0, largest = 1;
        while (x > 1) {
            int p = spf[x];
            distinct++;
            largest = p;
            while (x % p == 0) {
                total++;
                x /= p;
            }
        }
        cout << distinct << ' ' << total << ' ' << largest << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys


def spf_table(n: int) -> list[int]:
    spf = list(range(n + 1))
    if n >= 1:
        spf[1] = 1
    for p in range(2, n + 1):
        if spf[p] == p and p * p <= n:
            for x in range(p * p, n + 1, p):
                if spf[x] == x:
                    spf[x] = p
    return spf
```

The full reference file in the section uses this table and the repeated
division loop described above.

# C. Divisor Queries

## Restatement

For each `x`, print the number of positive divisors.

## Algorithm

Factor with SPF. If:

```text
x = p1^e1 * p2^e2 * ... * pk^ek
```

then:

```text
tau(x) = (e1+1)(e2+1)...(ek+1)
```

## Correctness proof

Every divisor chooses an exponent for each prime factor independently. For
prime `pi`, there are `ei+1` choices: `0,1,...,ei`. Multiplying the independent
choice counts gives the formula. SPF factorization gives the correct exponents,
so the computed product is correct. `\square`

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    int q;
    if (!(cin >> q)) return 0;
    vector<int> values(q);
    int mx = 1;
    for (int &x : values) {
        cin >> x;
        mx = max(mx, x);
    }
    vector<int> spf(mx + 1);
    iota(spf.begin(), spf.end(), 0);
    if (mx >= 1) spf[1] = 1;
    for (long long p = 2; p <= mx; p++) {
        if (spf[p] == p && p * p <= mx) {
            for (long long x = p * p; x <= mx; x += p) {
                if (spf[x] == x) spf[x] = p;
            }
        }
    }
    for (int x : values) {
        int ans = 1;
        while (x > 1) {
            int p = spf[x];
            int exp = 0;
            while (x % p == 0) {
                exp++;
                x /= p;
            }
            ans *= exp + 1;
        }
        cout << ans << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys


def spf_table(n: int) -> list[int]:
    spf = list(range(n + 1))
    if n >= 1:
        spf[1] = 1
    for p in range(2, n + 1):
        if spf[p] == p and p * p <= n:
            for x in range(p * p, n + 1, p):
                if spf[x] == x:
                    spf[x] = p
    return spf
```

Then divide by `spf[x]`, count the exponent, and multiply the answer by
`exponent + 1`.

# Testing discussion

The random tests compare the optimized SPF solutions against slow trial
division for small values. Important fixed tests include:

```text
n = 1
x = 1
large prime near the limit
prime powers such as 64
numbers with several distinct primes such as 210
```

# What to carry forward

Use primality sieves for prime flags and prefix counts. Use SPF tables when you
must factor many values. Once factorized, many divisor properties become simple
formulas over prime exponents.
